questions.q: Veltrix's invoices sometimes don't match the sales quote. What does this lesson identify as the actual root cause?
options: CPQ is calculating the wrong price
A manual re-keying handoff between CPQ and the finance system, with nothing enforcing the handoff happened correctly
The usage-based add-on is mathematically impossible to bill accurately
Salesforce does not support subscription pricing at all
questions.explain: The quote itself is calculated correctly in CPQ; the mismatch comes from the unautomated handoff where a human manually re-keys the quote's numbers into a separate billing system, with no check that the re-keyed values match.

questions.q: In the quote-to-cash chain this lesson describes, which system is authoritative for the negotiated products, discounts, and approved pricing?
options: The billing system
The customer's own records
CPQ
The usage-ingestion system
questions.explain: CPQ is the system of record for the negotiated quote itself — products, discounts, and approved pricing — while a contract/order record and a billing system are authoritative for later stages of the same chain.

questions.q: Why can't a mid-term seat increase simply be handled by re-running the original quote-to-cash process from scratch?
options: Because renewals and amendments are the exact same thing
Because Salesforce does not allow any change to an active subscription
Because seat increases are always rejected by CPQ
Because amendments need to update the active subscription's billing schedule with an auditable link back to the original contract, not restart the whole chain
questions.explain: An amendment needs to update the existing active subscription's billing schedule and stay traceable back to the original contract — re-running the entire original quote-to-cash chain from scratch isn't how a mid-term change to an already-active subscription should be modeled.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call usage-based billing an architecture change rather than just a different number in the price book?
options: Because it requires a usage-ingestion path feeding consumption data into billing on a cadence, plus a proration/true-up rule — surface area with no equivalent in flat-fee pricing
Because usage-based products cannot be quoted in CPQ at all
Because usage-based billing eliminates the need for a contract
Because flat-fee and usage-based pricing use an identical billing calculation
questions.explain: Flat-fee pricing is decided once at quote time; usage-based pricing depends on something that happens continuously during the billing period, which requires a whole new ingestion and true-up mechanism that a flat-fee design never needed.

questions.q: What is this lesson's point about treating amendments and renewals as rare edge cases in a subscription-billing design?
options: They genuinely are rare, so minimal design effort is justified
For an annual-subscription business, most of the install base eventually goes through a mid-term change, so skipping this is a design gap that will surface broadly, not an edge case
Renewals never actually require any system support, since customers always cancel instead
Amendments only ever happen to the top 1% of accounts by revenue
questions.explain: A design that only handles the initial new-sale quote and has no explicit model for amendments and renewals will work in a demo and then break for most subscriptions eventually, since mid-term changes are the normal lifecycle of a subscription business, not a rare exception.
